messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 79
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:


Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi Patel was a 79-year-old South Asian man who came to treatment after decades of trying to carry his wartime memories on his own. He had spent most of his adult life working in warehouses, sorting, lifting, and loading freight, and even now, despite his age and slowing pace, he still preferred the familiar order of boxes, pallets, and lists to sitting idle with his thoughts. He was divorced and lived alone, and the quiet hours after work had become the hardest part of the day. Ravi described his military service as the period that still divided his life into before and after. He had been in combat as a young man, and one incident in particular remained vivid: the sudden chaos of gunfire, the sharp cracking sounds, the smell of smoke and dust, and the instant sense that nowhere was safe. He remembered the moment as if it were still happening around him, not as a settled story from the past but as something that could break into the present without warning.

After he returned home, Ravi found that his mind would not leave the battlefield in the same way the rest of his life had moved on. He began to have repeated dreams in which he was back in the middle of the fighting, hearing the same bursts of gunfire and feeling the same surge of alarm before waking abruptly, often sweaty and tense. He also found himself dragged back by sudden reminders in everyday life. A loud bang in the warehouse, the slam of a metal door, or even the sharp crack of a pallet breaking apart could strike him like a blow and make him flinch before he had time to think. On some occasions, the reaction was strong enough that he felt as though he were back there for a moment, no longer in the warehouse but in the combat zone. He would look up quickly, scanning the room as if danger might be coming from anywhere.

Ravi said that one of the hardest things was the way memories could intrude without invitation. At times, while he was stacking inventory or walking down an aisle between shelves, a sound, a smell, or a brief image would pull him straight back to the war. He did not experience these as ordinary recollections. They came with force and vividness, and he described them as if they arrived fully formed, with the noise, the fear, and the helplessness attached. He often found himself upset by those moments and annoyed that they could still seize him so many years later. He had come to distrust his own mind because it seemed capable of dropping him into the past when he least expected it.

Because of this, Ravi gradually built his days around keeping as much distance as possible from reminders. He stayed away from war films and news coverage of conflict, and he would leave a room if conversations turned to fighting or military stories. In the warehouse, he chose tasks that allowed him to keep moving and avoid standing still in places where sudden noise might catch him off guard. He was careful around equipment and loading bays, where metal impacts and shouting were common, and he often positioned himself so he could see what was happening around him. Over time, this narrowed the way he worked. He became more isolated on the job, less likely to chat with co-workers, and more likely to keep to himself through the shift. At home, he spent long stretches alone and limited what he watched or listened to, hoping that if he could keep reminders out of reach, the old scenes would stay quieter.

Even so, Ravi remained on alert in a way that exhausted him. He was constantly listening for sudden noises and watching for anything that might signal trouble. He described being jumpy when he was startled, and his body would react before he could calm himself. He often felt keyed up and found it difficult to relax, especially in unfamiliar spaces or around unexpected sounds. The warehouse, with its clattering, echoing environment, kept him tense from the moment he arrived. He said he could never fully settle there, because part of him was always braced for the next loud sound. That state had become so familiar that he no longer noticed how much energy it took until the end of the day, when he was left drained and irritable.

Ravi also spoke of the way the war had changed how he saw himself and the world. He had come to believe that the world could turn dangerous without notice and that even ordinary sounds could hide something threatening. He carried a lasting sense that he had never really returned from combat, because in his mind the war remained unfinished. At times he felt detached from other people, as if they lived in a different reality from the one he inhabited. His divorce and solitary routine had left him with few opportunities to talk about any of this, and for years he kept functioning by staying busy and avoiding what he could.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was the growing strain of living this way at 79. The repeated nighttime dreams, the sharp reactions to bangs at work, and the exhaustion of constant watchfulness had become harder to dismiss. He no longer wanted to spend his remaining years bracing for explosions in a warehouse aisle or waking from the same war in the middle of the night. He came hoping for some relief from the memories that still ambushed him and from the fear that one loud sound would pull him back into the combat zone all over again.
